strengths: Originality: Modeling images as discretized, randomly deformed templates offers a useful statistical perspective on why higher resolution can improve classification despite increasing the ambient dimension. The contribution lies primarily in this understanding, with appropriate connections to registration and pattern theory.

Significance: The alignment classifier is simple and interpretable. Lemma A.2 and Theorem 3.4 connect support geometry and discretization error to classification with one training example per class under suitable separation conditions. This is a potentially useful account of how known invariances reduce sample requirements.

Presentation, limitations, and ethics: The progression from the generative model to alignment and CNN classifiers is accessible, with explanatory figures and detailed proof appendices. Sections 3 and 6 candidly discuss noise, partial visibility, and richer deformations. The MNIST experiments raise no apparent material ethical concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness: Theorems 4.1–4.2 omit the upper bound |ξ|, |ξ′| ≤ Ξ used in the proof of Proposition B.3. Assumption 1′ permits ξ = ξ′ = d and τ = τ′ = 0, which makes every sampled pixel zero because the templates are supported in [1/4,3/4]^2. Thus even separated templates can generate identical blank images, and input normalization becomes undefined. Explicit scale restrictions and corrected arguments are essential to the central CNN guarantees.

Soundness: The filter construction in the proof of Theorem 4.2 (p. 35) evaluates templates at unshifted coordinates over a grid containing zero and negative scales. When either scale is nonpositive, all sampled values vanish and the normalization denominator is zero. Omitting these filters would not establish the claimed treatment of flips. Separately, the unrestricted softmax least-squares argmin in (17) need not exist: on separable data, scaling the logits drives the loss toward zero without attaining it at finite weights. A valid filter construction and an approximate or suitably constrained minimization formulation are needed.

Soundness and optimality: Theorem 3.5 lower-bounds an unnormalized L2 distance for one specified deformation, whereas Theorem 3.4 uses the normalized separation D defined through infima over deformations. The lower-bound argument does not establish D ≳ 1/d or verify the same uniform Γ-set regularity required by the upper bound. Consequently, the claimed matching necessity of the separation condition is not established.

Empirical evidence: Section 5 fixes d = 28 and varies training size only from 2 to 64. Its CNNs use architectures substantially different from the analyzed global-max-pooling construction. Figure 5 supports the alignment method's advantage on these controlled tasks, but does not validate the resolution dependence, separation rates, or CNN learning guarantee. This matters because the manuscript claims that the experiments corroborate its theoretical findings.

Reproducibility: Although architectures, an optimizer, and 30 repetitions are reported, the manuscript omits essential details including augmentation ranges, training epochs, batch sizes, and precise template selection. No implementation availability is stated, and reporting medians without dispersion limits assessment of experimental variability.

Presentation and quantitative accuracy: Substituting n ≍ d^(4+q) log^4(d) into equation (18) yields a d^(-q/2) bound, rather than the stated d^(-q). The stronger conclusion needs an additional argument or different sample-size scaling. The classification rule on p. 13 also incorrectly thresholds the estimated class probability at zero instead of 1/2. These errors warrant correction alongside the substantive proof gaps.
